title: AgentNoiseBench: Benchmarking Robustness of Tool-Using LLM Agents Under Noisy Condition
one_liner: Test tool-using agents under controlled user and tool noise so we can measure how brittle they are outside ideal benchmark conditions.
lead: Many agent benchmarks assume clean instructions, clean tool outputs, and orderly interaction. Real use is messier. Users mistype requests, omit details, change goals midstream, or ask in confusing language. Tools can return partial outputs, stale data, or malformed results. This paper builds a benchmark pipeline that injects such noise in a controlled way so that we can measure how sensitive current agents are to imperfect conditions.

problem.h2: Benchmark agents look stronger than deployed agents because the test world is too clean
paras: An agent can score well in a benchmark where the user request is tidy and every tool behaves perfectly. That same agent may struggle in deployment because the real interaction contains ambiguity, typo-like noise, missing fields, delayed answers, and occasional tool mistakes.

If evaluation ignores those disturbances, it overstates practical quality. The paper studies a benchmark framework that injects controlled noise while keeping tasks solvable, so that evaluation can measure how quickly performance falls as the environment becomes less clean.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Take existing agent tasks, add controlled user-side and tool-side noise, and measure the drop in task success because deployment quality depends on how well the agent handles imperfect interaction.

panels.title: 1. A benchmark starts clean
panels.viz_args: Clear user request, tidy tool outputs, no interruptions.
panels.caption: Many published evaluations assume this ideal setting.

panels.title: 2. Real use is messier
panels.viz_args: Requests are incomplete and tools sometimes return odd or partial results.
panels.caption: Agents face this every day, so a clean-only benchmark misses an important failure mode.

panels.title: 3. Noise is injected deliberately
panels.caption: The framework controls the disturbance level so that comparisons stay fair across models.

panels.title: 4. The task remains solvable
panels.viz_args: Noise is added without destroying the underlying path to the answer.
panels.caption: That matters because evaluation should test resilience, not impossible tasks.

panels.title: 5. Sensitivity becomes visible
panels.viz_args: Different agents lose quality at different rates as noise rises.
panels.caption: The benchmark reveals which systems depend too heavily on perfect interaction.

steps.text: Group messy interaction into user-side noise and tool-side noise so that the benchmark reflects common deployment problems.
Modify existing agent tasks with adjustable disturbance while preserving solvability because the goal is to test resilience, not create impossible cases.
Run diverse models across noise levels so that sensitivity can be compared under the same task conditions.
Track how quickly task success falls as user or tool noise increases because steep drop means the agent depends on unrealistic cleanliness.
Separate user-side and tool-side effects so that future work can target the true weakness.

paras: The paper changes the evaluation environment. Instead of measuring only ideal-condition task accuracy, it measures how gracefully performance degrades when the interaction becomes noisy but still solvable.
object.object: the benchmark condition under which agent quality is measured

hidden.name: how much useful task progress survives after noise is introduced
paras: The central hidden quantity is noise tolerance. You do not observe it directly from one clean benchmark score because clean success says little about what happens once the request or tool output becomes messy.

You estimate it by increasing disturbance and watching how much useful task progress remains. A tolerant agent should recover from missing details or odd tool outputs because it can ask clarifying questions, verify results, and avoid overcommitting to one brittle interpretation.

heat.caption: The darkest cells are the moments where disturbance forces the agent to recover instead of blindly continuing.

reads.html: The hidden question is how much work the agent can still get done once the interaction becomes messy.
Noise-tolerant agents preserve task progress under disturbed inputs and outputs, which means their deployment behavior is less tied to ideal benchmark cleanliness.

mechanism.h2: Why controlled noise injection reveals real weaknesses
paras: A single clean benchmark score bundles many abilities together and hides whether the agent can recover from minor disturbance. Controlled noise injection separates that question out because it changes only the cleanliness of the interaction while preserving the underlying task.

The split between user-side and tool-side noise is also important. Those two sources demand different recovery behavior. User-side noise requires clarification and goal tracking, while tool-side noise requires verification and fallback handling. A benchmark that distinguishes them can show exactly where an agent breaks.

stages.s: Inject user-side and tool-side disturbance while keeping tasks solvable
Run agents across several disturbance levels
Measure success drop by disturbance type
A clearer view of deployment sensitivity

math.h2: A compact way to summarize noise tolerance
math.words: Noise tolerance can be viewed as clean-task success minus the performance drop under disturbance, because a better agent keeps more of its original ability when the interaction gets messy.
symbols: remaining useful ability after accounting for disturbance sensitivity
how much success falls after user or tool noise is introduced

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an agent reaches 90 success in a clean benchmark.
After moderate disturbance, its success falls to 62, so the drop is 28.
Then its noise tolerance score is 62 by this simple summary, which is 90 minus 28.
Another agent that falls only to 76 would have a smaller drop of 14.
That second agent looks stronger under deployment-style conditions because it preserves more of its clean-task ability.

math.note: The paper reports fuller benchmark results, but this summary captures the main question: how much quality survives once noise arrives.

charts.title: Ideal-condition evaluation
charts.note: Clean-only tests can still be useful, but they hide how agents behave once normal imperfections appear.

charts.title: Noise-injected evaluation
charts.note: The lower raw success is informative because it exposes failures that clean evaluation was masking.

items.b: Badly designed noise can make tasks unrealistic.
items.html: If the disturbance does not resemble real user or tool problems, the benchmark may punish models for artificial quirks because the injected cases are not representative of deployment.

items.b: Too much disturbance can destroy solvability.
items.html: If essential task information is removed entirely, failure no longer measures resilience because even a good recovery policy has nothing left to work with.

items.b: One summary number can hide which source of noise hurt most.
items.html: An aggregate score may blur user-side and tool-side weaknesses, so separate reporting matters because fixes for those weaknesses are different.
The benchmark is most useful when it preserves solvability and tags the disturbance source, because then failure traces point to concrete recovery gaps.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take an existing tool-using benchmark and add a switchable noise layer. On the user side, introduce missing fields, reordered intent, and ambiguous wording. On the tool side, introduce partial outputs, stale values, and malformed returns while keeping the task solvable. Run several agents at each disturbance level.

The demo should show both the success drop and the recovery behavior. A better agent should ask clarifying questions, retry when needed, and cross-check suspicious outputs because those actions preserve useful progress under noise.
demo.metric_eq: tolerance_gap = clean_success - noisy_success ; recovery_gain = recovered_tasks_after_checks - recovered_tasks_without_checks
demo.closing: The point of the demo is to show that deployment readiness depends on noise tolerance because real interactions are rarely as clean as a benchmark prompt.
